newsitem.title: USA: BARSHEFSKY SEES "INTENSE" EFFORT ON FAST-TRACK.
newsitem.headline: BARSHEFSKY SEES "INTENSE" EFFORT ON FAST-TRACK.

text.p: The Clinton administration faces a "very intense and busy fall" trying to win congressional approval to begin "fast-track" trade negotiations with Chile and other Latin American nations, a top U.S. official said Wednesday.
"When the fall begins with fast track, things are going to get very crazy," U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told reporters at a briefing on trade issues.
The administration will put together its fast track proposal over "the next 2 or 3 weeks" and submit the bill to Congress in "early September," Barshefsky said.

It will consult with members of both parties in the House and the Senate and with business, labor and environmental groups to fashion a bill that is broad enough to win congressional approval, she said.
But whether the administration can put together a bill that acheives broad bipartisan support is far from certain.
Key Democrats have insisted on including environmental and labor issues in the trade negotiations, while Republicans are opposed to those additions.
That standoff is one reason why the administration has not yet submitted fast-track legislation.
In the meantime, President Clinton has continued to call on Congress to give him the authority to begin talks with Chile on joining the free-trade pact with the U.S., Canada and Mexico.
Eventually, the U.S. hopes to expand the North American Free Trade Agreement throughout Central and South America.
Congress will have a say in which countries would be next in line for negotiations after Chile, Barshefsky said.
"The administration will not put together a bill in a vacuum," Barshefsky said, acknowledging that they will need both Democratic and Republican votes to win approval.
